prompt: What are the obstacles to mental excellence named in the passage?

options.text: Sin, accepting the status quo, the trap of past failures, the pride of past achievements, comparison, and the fear of curses and enchantments
Sin, idleness, poverty, fear, doubt and pride
Fear, anxiety, concerns, noise, crowds and haste
Sin, pride, comparison and the love of money

explanation: Six headings in the chapter, in this order. The pride of past achievements is explicitly called the fourth, which fixes the sequence.

why.a: Correct. These six are the chapter's headings, in order.
why.b: Wrong. Poverty and doubt are never treated as obstacles in this book.
why.c: Wrong. Fear, anxiety and concerns are the enemies of INSPIRATION in Chapter 6, a different list.
why.d: Wrong. It drops three and adds the love of money, which the book never names as an obstacle to mental excellence.

prompt: Why does the enemy organize obstacles against the mind?

options.text: Because your mind is the gateway to your life, so when it is blinded your destiny is blocked and your future becomes uncertain
Because the mind is the weakest part of a man
Because he cannot touch the spirit of a believer
Because thoughts are easier to disguise than actions

explanation: The gateway image comes straight from Chapter 1, and 2 Corinthians 4:3-4 supplies the blinding: the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not.

why.a: Correct. The gateway logic is the reason given, and the devil is called a mind-blocker.
why.b: Wrong. The book calls the mind a great treasure and the factor that makes you relevant, not a weak point.
why.c: Wrong. No such limitation on the enemy is stated.
why.d: Wrong. Concealment is not the reason offered.

prompt: How does the passage describe what the devil does to drug addicts?

options.text: He plays on their minds by deceiving them to try out pleasures, and in trying out pleasures they multiply pressures for themselves
He binds them with a spirit of addiction
He isolates them from every good influence
He removes their ability to choose

explanation: The pleasures and pressures rhyme is the hook, and it matches Chapter 8's line that many read for pleasure and no wonder they live under pressure.

why.a: Correct. The route is through the mind and through pleasure, and it ends in multiplied pressure.
why.b: Wrong. A spirit of addiction is standard deliverance language the book does not use.
why.c: Wrong. Isolation is not mentioned, and the book actually commends solitude for other purposes.
why.d: Wrong. The devil is said to work by tricks and gimmicks because he has lost all his power.

prompt: How does the passage describe Adam before the fall?

options.text: A symbol of supernatural mental excellence who knew almost everything and single-handedly named all the animals
A man who walked with God but had no knowledge of good and evil
A gardener given a simple task and a simple mind
The first prophet, who spoke with God face to face

explanation: The naming of the animals is offered as the proof of his mental excellence, which makes his post-fall failure the sharper: he could think of no covering but leaves.

why.a: Correct. Both claims are made, and the naming of all the animals is the evidence given.
why.b: Wrong. Innocence is not the emphasis; mental excellence is.
why.c: Wrong. This is the opposite of the passage's picture of him.
why.d: Wrong. Prophecy is not part of the description.

prompt: What does the passage make of Adam covering himself with leaves after he had sinned?

options.text: That with all the creative ability of God inside him he could find no better covering, because he had stepped out of mental excellence
That he was ashamed and acted in haste
That leaves were all that was available to him
That he was trying to hide from God rather than to clothe himself

explanation: It is the evidence for the claim that sin corrupts mentality: the same man who named all the animals could not think of anything better than leaves.

why.a: Correct. The contrast between his creative ability and the poverty of his solution is the argument.
why.b: Wrong. Shame and haste are the usual reading, and not the one this book makes.
why.c: Wrong. Availability would excuse him, which would destroy the point.
why.d: Wrong. Hiding is a separate part of the story that the passage does not use.

prompt: What did Dr. T. L. Osborn say about sin, as quoted in this chapter?

options.text: "Every time you sin, something dies in you"
"When you stop learning, you start dying"
"Sin is the thief of destiny"
"No man sins in isolation"

explanation: The author adds his own gloss: one of the things that die in people when they sin is their heritage of mental excellence. Ezekiel 18:4 backs it, 'The soul that sinneth, it shall die.'

why.a: Correct. This is Osborn's second quotation in the book, and it belongs to this chapter.
why.b: Wrong. That is Osborn's OTHER line, quoted in Chapters 2 and 8 about learning.
why.c: Wrong. An invented saying in the right register.
why.d: Wrong. Also invented; the book makes no such claim.

prompt: What two things does the passage say Joseph did NOT do in Potiphar's house?

options.text: He did not attempt to escape from slavery though he knew the way home, and he did not play around with his master's substance
He did not complain about his treatment, and he did not seek revenge on his brothers
He did not reveal his identity, and he did not ask for freedom
He did not defend himself when accused, and he did not curse his accusers

explanation: The escape point is the striking one: he was grown enough to know the way back home, yet he never attempted it. The conclusion is that every man of integrity naturally enjoys mental dignity.

why.a: Correct. Both restraints are named, and the passage stresses that he knew the way home.
why.b: Wrong. The brothers do not appear in this book's use of Joseph.
why.c: Wrong. Concealed identity is not part of the account here.
why.d: Wrong. The accusation and imprisonment are not discussed at this point.

prompt: What does the passage call sin in relation to Satan's strategy?

options.text: Satan's number one trap, by which he drags you into the net of mental failure
Satan's last resort when other methods fail
Satan's way of testing a believer's resolve
Satan's means of separating believers from one another

explanation: It closes the section, following the claim that many believers are dead mentally and continue killing themselves gradually until they are completely dead.

why.a: Correct. Number one trap, and the net of mental failure is the image used.
why.b: Wrong. It is ranked first, not last.
why.c: Wrong. Testing is not a category the book applies to the devil.
why.d: Wrong. Division among believers is never discussed.

prompt: What warning does the passage give about pushing?

options.text: The moment you stop pushing, you start crashing
Push only as hard as grace allows
Pushing without direction wastes strength
The one who pushes longest wins

explanation: It is the answer to the thought the enemy plants: 'This is where I belong. God has tried. This is just okay.' Proverbs 4:18 backs it, that the path of the just shines more and more unto the perfect day.

why.a: Correct. Stop pushing, start crashing, with no middle state of holding steady.
why.b: Wrong. Grace is required for inspiration in Chapter 6, but no limit on effort is set.
why.c: Wrong. Direction matters in Chapter 2, but this line is about not stopping.
why.d: Wrong. Endurance framing is not what this sentence says.

prompt: Why does accepting the status quo paralyse a person, according to the passage?

options.text: Because only those who see what lies ahead take steps toward it, so if you cannot see anything ahead you take no steps and life grinds to a halt
Because contentment removes the desire to pray
Because God withdraws His blessing from the passive
Because others overtake you and you lose heart

explanation: It ties back to Chapter 2's imagination material, that until you see it God cannot give it. The related claim is that nothing motivates the brain to work like seeing something ahead of you.

why.a: Correct. Sight precedes steps, so blocked sight stops movement.
why.b: Wrong. Prayer is not the faculty in view.
why.c: Wrong. Withdrawal of blessing is not stated here.
why.d: Wrong. Comparison with others is a SEPARATE obstacle, the fifth one.

prompt: What point does the passage make with Kenneth Hagin's books on healing?

options.text: The one he wrote in 1996 was more powerful than the one he wrote in 1960, thirty-six years before
He wrote the same book twice because the need had not changed
His later book corrected the errors of his earlier one
He stopped writing on healing after his first book

explanation: It illustrates Proverbs 4:18, the path of the just shining more and more with each passing day, and it is offered against accepting where you are now as your limit.

why.a: Correct. 1996 and 1960, thirty-six years apart, with the later one more powerful and far more loaded.
why.b: Wrong. The point is growth, not repetition.
why.c: Wrong. Correction is not mentioned; increase in power is.
why.d: Wrong. He wrote a second, which is the whole example.

prompt: What examples does the passage give of the irreparable past that Satan connects people to?

options.text: The car that had an accident and was a write-off, and the exam you wrote and failed
The friend who betrayed you and the money you lost
The years you wasted and the calling you ignored
The sickness you suffered and the debt you carried

explanation: Two concrete examples, both losses that cannot be undone, which is why the section calls the past irreparable and tells you to leave it in the grave.

why.a: Correct. The written-off car and the failed exam are the two given.
why.b: Wrong. Betrayal is never discussed in this book.
why.c: Wrong. Wasted years and ignored calling are not the examples used.
why.d: Wrong. Debt is discussed in Chapter 5, but not as an example of the past to forget.

prompt: What does the passage say will happen if you do not let the past be past?

options.text: You are likely to pass away with it, so bury the past otherwise you will be buried along with it
You will repeat the same failure again
You will pass the burden to your children
You will lose the lesson the failure was meant to teach

explanation: The wordplay on past and pass away carries it, and Philippians 3:13-14 supplies the model: forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before.

why.a: Correct. Both halves are in the text, and the burial image is repeated.
why.b: Wrong. Repetition is not the consequence named.
why.c: Wrong. Inheritance of a burden is closer to the imagined ailment in Chapter 2.
why.d: Wrong. The book says anything negative is not worthy of a place in your memory bank, so it is not after lessons from failure.

topic: a just man falleth seven times
prompt: Which scripture is quoted as "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again"?

options.text: Proverbs 24:16
Micah 7:8
Proverbs 4:18
Philippians 3:13

explanation: Proverbs 24:16. Micah 7:8 is quoted in the same section but says something different: 'when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.'

why.a: Correct. Proverbs 24:16 is the seven times verse.
why.b: Wrong. Micah 7:8 is the companion verse a few lines later, addressed to an enemy.
why.c: Wrong. Proverbs 4:18 is the shining light verse, used under accepting the status quo.
why.d: Wrong. Philippians 3:13-14 is forgetting what is behind and pressing toward the mark.

prompt: What two illustrations does the passage use for rising after a fall?

options.text: No world champion in wrestling was never once on the floor, and you will never find a general who has no scars
A runner who stumbles and a swimmer who tires
A farmer whose first crop fails and a builder whose wall collapses
A ship in a storm and a tree in a wind

explanation: The general has two or three stars on his shoulder at the end despite the scars, and the champion's arms are still raised in victory even with blood dripping from his nostrils.

why.a: Correct. The wrestler and the general are the two, both drawn from contest and combat.
why.b: Wrong. Neither appears in the book.
why.c: Wrong. Farming and building are used elsewhere, but not for this point.
why.d: Wrong. Storms appear only in the phrase about finding your way out of any storm, in Chapter 1.

prompt: What does the passage say should be kept in remembrance?

options.text: Your testimonies, not your trials, because anything negative paralyzes mentality
Both your victories and your defeats, so you learn from each
The mercies of God rather than your own achievements
The promises you have not yet seen fulfilled

explanation: 'If there's anything to remember in the past, let it be your great successes, accomplishments and great results.' Anything negative is said to be unworthy of a place in your memory bank.

why.a: Correct. Testimonies rather than trials, and the reason is that the negative paralyzes mentality.
why.b: Wrong. Learning from defeat sounds wise, but the book rules the negative out entirely.
why.c: Wrong. This is a pious-sounding alternative the passage does not offer.
why.d: Wrong. Unfulfilled promises are not the subject here.

topic: the man who will not fly
prompt: What example does the passage give of a man whose mentality was dulled by the past?

options.text: An educated elderly man who never travels by plane because he has seen one or two crashes, though there are more car accidents than plane crashes
A businessman who never trades again after one loss
A student who never sits another exam after failing once
A minister who stops preaching after a rejected sermon

explanation: The detail that makes it sting is that he is educated and can afford to fly, and that he would rather travel by road on long journeys. So even if something good waited for him in Canada, he would not go.

why.a: Correct. The aeroplane example is the one given, with Canada named as the forgone opportunity.
why.b: Wrong. Business losses are not used this way.
why.c: Wrong. A failed exam is mentioned as a memory to bury, but no such man is described.
why.d: Wrong. No such minister appears.

prompt: What does the passage say about what appears standard today?

options.text: It very soon becomes sub-standard tomorrow
It should be defended against every change
It was won at a cost others do not see
It is a gift rather than an achievement

explanation: The fourth obstacle is the pride of past achievements, which paralyses your drive and mentality and stunts your growth. Micah 2:10 is quoted: this is not your rest, because it is polluted.

why.a: Correct. Standard today, sub-standard tomorrow, which is why past achievement cannot be a resting place.
why.b: Wrong. Defending the present is precisely the fault being named.
why.c: Wrong. The cost of past success is not the subject.
why.d: Wrong. The passage says to bless God for past achievement, but its point is about moving on.

prompt: Which idiomatic expression does the passage cite against the pride of past achievements?

options.text: One shouldn't rest on one's oars
Don't count your chickens before they hatch
A rolling stone gathers no moss
Don't put new wine in old bottles

explanation: 'There is this idiomatic expression that says one shouldn't rest on one's oars. It means don't dwell too much on past achievements.' The book explains the idiom immediately, which is how you know it is the one.

why.a: Correct. Resting on one's oars, glossed as dwelling on past achievements.
why.b: Wrong. A common idiom the book does not use.
why.c: Wrong. Also common, also absent.
why.d: Wrong. That is a biblical saying rather than an idiom, and it is not quoted here.

topic: when your assignment becomes a task
prompt: In which of his own books does the author say that when your assignment becomes a task, all your senses will come alive?

options.text: Towards Excellence in Life & Ministry
Dynamics Of Holiness
Signposts On The Road to Success
Towards Mental Exploits

explanation: Two of his own books are named in this text: Towards Excellence in Life & Ministry here, and Dynamics Of Holiness in the testimony in Chapter 8.

why.a: Correct. This is the book cited for that line.
why.b: Wrong. Dynamics Of Holiness is the book Bishop Abioye recommended in the testimony in Chapter 8.
why.c: Wrong. Signposts On The Road to Success is E. W. Kenyon's book.
why.d: Wrong. That is the title of the book you are reading, and it does not cite itself here.

prompt: What does the passage say about those who pitched their tents mentally?

options.text: They are not moving forward any more, and if you pitch your tent too early you will lose relevance in no time
They have found the place God intended for them
They will be moved on by circumstances eventually
They should be encouraged rather than criticised

explanation: The concrete example is the ministers who started with him and are still renting chairs and negotiating with landlords, because they felt this is the place to pitch our tent.

why.a: Correct. Both halves are stated, including the phrase lose relevance in no time.
why.b: Wrong. This is the very self-deception the section attacks.
why.c: Wrong. The passage says they stall, not that circumstances will rescue them.
why.d: Wrong. The tone is a warning throughout.

prompt: What distinction does the passage say you must know in order not to lose relevance?

options.text: The difference between the time to rent and the time to be a house owner
The difference between a calling and a career
The difference between a season of rest and a season of work
The difference between a gift and a skill

explanation: 'But there is a time to rent and another time to be a house owner. If you don't know the difference between the two timings, you will lose relevance.' It follows the example of ministers still renting chairs.

why.a: Correct. Renting against owning, and the word the book uses is timings.
why.b: Wrong. Calling and career are not categories in this book.
why.c: Wrong. Rest is not commended anywhere as a season here; Micah 2:10 says this is not your rest.
why.d: Wrong. The gift and its development are discussed in Chapter 8, not here.

prompt: What are the two sides of the trap of comparison?

options.text: Comparing yourself with those more privileged, asking 'Can I ever get there?', and with those less privileged, saying 'I think I have tried'
Comparing your gifts with others, and comparing your trials with others
Comparing your past with your present, and your present with your hopes
Comparing yourself with believers, and with unbelievers

explanation: Both directions are traps, and each is given its own inner monologue. 2 Corinthians 10:12 supplies the text, that they measuring themselves by themselves are not wise.

why.a: Correct. Upward and downward comparison, with the exact self-talk the book supplies for each.
why.b: Wrong. Gifts and trials are not the axes named.
why.c: Wrong. Time comparison belongs to the past failures and past achievements obstacles.
why.d: Wrong. The believer and unbeliever comparison appears in the Introduction, and for a different purpose.

prompt: What did Jesus say to Peter when Peter asked "What about this man?"

options.text: If it is my wish that the man tarries till I come, what's your business?
Feed my sheep, and follow thou me
It is not for you to know the times or the seasons
Judge not, that ye be not judged

explanation: Cited to John 21:20-22, and paired with 1 Thessalonians 4:11, 'Study to be quiet and do your own business.' Both are used against comparison.

why.a: Correct. This is the reply as the book paraphrases it, and the sting is in 'what's your business'.
why.b: Wrong. A genuine line from the same chapter of John that the book does not quote here.
why.c: Wrong. That is from Acts and is not used in this book.
why.d: Wrong. Another real saying that does not appear.

prompt: What does the passage say the privileges around you are?

options.text: Pointers to the mission that God has ordained you to accomplish
Rewards for faithfulness already shown
Tests of whether you will remain humble
Evidence that God has forgiven your past

explanation: It is paired with the principle that much is expected from whom much is given, cited to Luke 12:48, and with the principle of identity: you are here on a mission.

why.a: Correct. Privileges point to mission, which is why comparison with others is beside the point.
why.b: Wrong. Reward framing is not used.
why.c: Wrong. Testing is not how the book reads privilege.
why.d: Wrong. Forgiveness is not the subject of this passage.

prompt: What does the passage say about curses and the redeemed?

options.text: Curses and enchantments have lost their hold, so you cannot be cursed, molested, enchanted or bewitched
Curses can still operate if there is unconfessed sin
Curses must be broken by a minister before they lose power
Curses affect the body but not the mind

explanation: Galatians 3:13-14 and Genesis 12:3 are the grounds: Christ redeemed us from the curse, and you are now connected to the blessing channel of Abraham.

why.a: Correct. All four verbs are used, and the claim is unqualified for the redeemed.
why.b: Wrong. No such condition is attached, and adding one would undo the argument.
why.c: Wrong. No ministerial action is required in this account.
why.d: Wrong. The chapter's whole concern is the MIND, and it says fear of curses is what stops people thinking.

topic: the man who fasted forty days
prompt: How does the passage describe the man who believes a curse is working against him?

options.text: Whatever he hears in church bounces back, he despises what he reads, and he has fasted forty days over the matter without giving it a thought for one second
He seeks out deliverance ministers year after year
He blames his parents for what he has become
He refuses to attend church at all

explanation: The contrast between forty days of fasting and not one second of thought is the sharpest line in the section, and it fits the book's running argument that thinking is what people skip.

why.a: Correct. All three details are given, and the forty days against one second is the punchline.
why.b: Wrong. Deliverance ministry is never mentioned in this book.
why.c: Wrong. He blames a curse from the fourth generation, not his parents personally.
why.d: Wrong. He does hear things in church; they simply bounce back.

topic: the witch at the filling station
prompt: What did the author reply to the woman who told him he would never get where he was going?

options.text: "As soon as I get there, you will hear"
"No weapon formed against me shall prosper"
"I rebuke you in the name of Jesus"
He said nothing and drove away

explanation: He had overtaken her on the highway and she met him at a filling station where he had stopped to refuel, snapping at him with gleaming eyes. The reply is confident rather than combative, which is the point.

why.a: Correct. This is the reply as printed, and its quiet confidence is why it is memorable.
why.b: Wrong. A real declaration but not the one used here.
why.c: Wrong. No rebuke is recorded, which matters because the passage is arguing that curses have no hold.
why.d: Wrong. He replied quickly, which the text says explicitly.

prompt: What word does the passage say is used to describe fear, and why?

options.text: Paranoid, because it has a paralysing effect on its victim
Bondage, because it holds a man against his will
Blindness, because it hides what is ahead
Poison, because it spreads through the whole man

explanation: The chapter ends on it: people who live in fear hardly think well, because fear paralyzes mentality. Fear is also one of the three enemies of inspiration in Chapter 6.

why.a: Correct. Paranoid is the word, and the paralysing effect is the reason given.
why.b: Wrong. Bondage is not the term used.
why.c: Wrong. Blinding is what the devil does to MINDS in 2 Corinthians 4:4, at the start of this chapter, and is a separate idea.
why.d: Wrong. Poison is not an image this book uses.

prompt: Fill the blank: "Sin corrupts {{1}}."
explanation: Mentality. The book keeps sin's damage in mental terms throughout the chapter, which is why the sentence does not say character or conscience.

prompt: The passage says the devil uses tricks and gimmicks because he has lost all his power.

options.text: True
False

explanation: True. 'He uses tricks and gimmicks in getting his results, because he has lost all his power.' Genesis 3:1 is cited for his subtlety, and the warning is that you cannot catch him easily except you are spiritually smart.

why.true: Correct. Powerlessness is precisely why he must work by deception, which is the chapter's theory of how obstacles operate.
why.false: Wrong. The book states this plainly, and it is what makes the mind the battleground rather than raw force.

prompt: Which scripture opens the chapter on obstacles?

options.text: 1 Corinthians 16:9
2 Corinthians 4:3-4
Genesis 3:1
Ezekiel 18:4

explanation: 1 Corinthians 16:9: 'For a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries.' The chapter's opening line is that every great door commands the attention of adversaries.

why.a: Correct. 1 Corinthians 16:9 is the opening text.
why.b: Wrong. 2 Corinthians 4:3-4 follows a few lines later, on the god of this world blinding minds.
why.c: Wrong. Genesis 3:1 on the serpent's subtlety comes later in the same introduction.
why.d: Wrong. Ezekiel 18:4 belongs to the section on sin.
